heading: Two enclaves, one flag change, and a very late merger
body: Long before India's states were redrawn along linguistic lines, a scatter of small Portuguese-held enclaves sat embedded inside British and princely India, tiny pockets of a European empire that had nothing to do with Goa's much larger colonial story next door. Daman (on the Gujarat coast) and Diu (an island off Kathiawar) had been Portuguese possessions since the 1500s, taken and fortified as way-stations on the sea route to Goa; Dadra and Nagar Haveli, an inland pocket further south, came under Portuguese control much later, from 1783-85, after a dispute settlement with the Maratha-era Peshwa administration. The two never formed a single administrative unit under the Portuguese — they were governed separately and only share a modern history because both were, for two centuries, small outposts of the same distant empire.

Their exits from Portuguese rule were also different, and accounts differ on how to characterise the first one. In July-August 1954, pro-merger activists and volunteers — accounts describe involvement from the Communist Party of India, the RSS and other nationalist groups — moved into Dadra and Nagar Haveli and displaced the Portuguese administration; the enclave then ran itself for seven years as the self-declared 'Free Dadra and Nagar Haveli' before formally acceding to India in 1961. Some press coverage instead names a specific group, the United Front of Goans, as responsible for the initial 22 July 1954 attack on the Dadra police post that began the takeover — this page has not independently confirmed that account against a more authoritative source, so take the named-organisation attribution as unresolved. Sources vary in whether they call this action a 'liberation' or, in the language used by some legal and historical accounts (including the case later heard at the International Court of Justice over Portuguese transit rights), an 'annexation' — the events themselves are well documented even where the label is contested. Daman and Diu followed a different, later and more clearly military path: they were taken by the Indian armed forces in December 1961 as part of the wider annexation of Portuguese India (alongside Goa), ending Portugal's presence in the subcontinent outright.

For the next few decades the two areas were administered separately: Dadra and Nagar Haveli as its own union territory from 1961, Daman and Diu bundled with Goa until Goa became a full state in 1987, after which Daman and Diu became a union territory in its own right. That arrangement lasted only until 2020: on 26 January of that year, a 2019 Act of Parliament merged the two union territories into a single administrative unit, Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu, purely for administrative efficiency rather than any deeper historical unity between them.

The places on this map from the territory reflect that layered past — Portuguese forts and churches on the coast at Daman and Diu, and the very different, inland, tribal-belt history of Dadra and Nagar Haveli, joined administratively only in living memory.
